sentences.text: Allosaurus was a large bipedal predator characterized by a massive skull, short neck, long tail, and reduced forelimbs.
Its skull was lightly built and, like its dozens of sharp, serrated teeth, modest in size compared with other theropods of its body size.
A 30 square centimeter skin impression of a juvenile Allosaurus was found associated with the anterior dorsal ribs and pectoral region.

A skin impression from the base of the tail of the "Big Al Two" specimen measures 20 by 20 centimeters and contains scales up to 2 centimeters in diameter, though researchers suggest these scales may belong to a sauropod rather than to Allosaurus.
The "Big Al Two" specimen also preserves a 20 by 20 centimeter skin impression from the underside of the neck, with scutate scales 0.5 centimeters wide and 11 centimeters long.
The specimen known as "Big Al" preserves 19 distinct pathologies across its skeleton.
The first definitive fossil remains of Allosaurus were described in 1877 by Othniel C. Marsh.
Allosaurus was discovered during the "Bone Wars," a rivalry between Othniel Charles Marsh and Edward Drinker Cope that spurred fossil discoveries in the Western US.

Antrodemus, the genus to which Joseph Leidy assigned the first fossil, was the accepted name for over 50 years until James H. Madsen argued that Allosaurus should be used due to the poor quality of Antrodemus's diagnostic material.
The International Commission on Zoological Nomenclature ratified a petition in December 2023 to designate specimen USNM 4734 as the neotype for Allosaurus fragilis.
As the most abundant large predator in the Morrison Formation, Allosaurus was an apex predator likely hunting ornithopods, stegosaurids, and sauropods.
Isotopic evidence suggests Allosaurus was an opportunistic predator that consumed Camarasaurus, Camptosaurus, and Diplodocus, though it is unclear whether it hunted or scavenged them.
Robert T. Bakker compared Allosaurus to Cenozoic saber-toothed mammals, noting adaptations like reduced jaw muscles, increased neck muscles, and the ability to open jaws extremely wide.

One study deems unlikely the "hatchet jaw" attack, in which Allosaurus would strike with its wide-open jaws, and reinterprets the wide gape as an adaptation for delivering muscle-driven bites to large prey, with weaker jaw muscles as the trade-off.
Evidence for cannibalism in Allosaurus includes shed teeth found among rib fragments and possible tooth marks on a shoulder blade.
Histological analysis suggests Allosaurus stopped growing at around 22 to 28 years of age, similar to other large theropods like Tyrannosaurus.
Madsen suggested that the unfused pubic bones of some Allosaurus belonged to females, as the gap would make egg-laying easier, but the idea has drawn little further attention.

In 1972, Kristen Petersen and colleagues documented pathologies in Cleveland-Lloyd Quarry specimens, including rib fractures, joint stiffness, fused tail vertebrae, and possible bite-induced bone amputations.
Allosaurus is classified within the family Allosauridae.
Allosaurus lived during the Kimmeridgian to Tithonian ages of the Late Jurassic period.
Statistical analyses between 1996 and 1999 suggested that variations in Allosaurus fossils from the Morrison Formation represent individual differences rather than distinct species.
The validity of the European species Allosaurus europaeus has been debated, with some studies suggesting it is a synonym of A. fragilis, a doubtful name, or requires re-evaluation.
